title: Greenwood Village Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Greenwood Village wells have a 35 ft median depth, but some reach 2,485 ft. See yield, water levels, costs and local well risks.
h1: Greenwood Village Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Greenwood Village sits on the plains over the Denver Basin, where nearby well records show a wide range of drilling conditions. The median reported depth is 35 feet, but the deepest recorded well reaches 2,485 feet. That spread matters when comparing a rural property, planning a new home, or reviewing a driller’s estimate.

This page covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Greenwood Village, including nearby Cherry Hills Village, Cherry Creek, Centennial, Holly Hills, Inverness, and Acres Green. The records include 4,911 wells, although only 2,145 are recorded as constructed, 2,636 report total depth, 230 report pump yield, and 81 report static water level.

sections.heading: Greenwood Village well depth depends on the formation
sections.html:
Most recorded wells near Greenwood Village are relatively shallow: 73% are under 100 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 23 to 120 feet, with a median of 35 feet. That is a useful local starting point, but not a guarantee for a particular lot.

The outliers are substantial. Seventeen percent of wells are 600 feet or deeper, the 90th-percentile depth is 1,072 feet, and the deepest record is 2,485 feet. Permits name the unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer most often, along with the Arapahoe and Alluvial aquifers. Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 100% of the listed aquifer records. A bid should be based on the parcel, nearby logs, casing and grout requirements, and the target aquifer—not just the local median.

sections.heading: How much water do Greenwood Village wells produce?
sections.html:
Reported pump yields have a median of 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 10.0 to 124.8 gallons per minute. Fifty-seven percent of the reported wells make more than 15 gallons per minute. Those figures indicate that strong wells are common in the records, but yield data exists for only 230 wells, so it is not a complete performance survey.

Low-producing wells still occur. Three percent report less than 1 gallon per minute, while 9% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. For a buyer, a low-yield result can affect storage, household use, irrigation plans, and financing. Ask for the well permit, construction report, pumping information, and any yield test rather than relying on a neighbor’s result.

sections.heading: The Greenwood Village water table looks fairly stable
sections.html:
Among the 81 wells reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 20 feet, with the middle half between 11 and 50 feet below the surface. That is a shallow water level compared with the full range of drilling depths, but static level and well depth are different measurements. A shallow water level does not mean every new well can be drilled shallow or will produce well.

The decade series does not show a dropping trend in these records. The median static level was 18 feet below surface in the 2010s and 17 feet in the 2020s. The sample is limited, so a property-specific measurement is still important. Confirm the static level, pump setting, and seasonal conditions in the well documents before treating the area trend as a guarantee.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Greenwood Village, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity has continued across several generations. Records show 126 permits from the 1950s, 133 from the 1960s, 263 from the 1970s, 288 from the 1980s, 1,064 from the 1990s, 1,164 from the 2000s, 550 from the 2010s, and 293 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 1,622 listed wells, followed by Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.) with 188 and Ground Exploration LLC (Bender, Joseph T.) with 104. These counts describe permit records, not endorsements or current availability. Before buying, pull nearby DWR permits and construction reports. They can show actual depths, casing, aquifer names, and reported performance closer to the lot.

sections.heading: What a new well costs in Greenwood Village
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone is estimated at about $1,800 to $2,400. That is only the drilling portion, not a ready-to-use water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $7,800 to $14,400 at the median depth. A deeper-than-expected hole can move the price well beyond that range, especially if casing, grout, access, difficult material, or a different completion design is needed. Get the contractor’s assumptions in writing: included depth, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, trench length, electrical work, permits, and the price for additional footage.

sections.heading: Environmental and construction checks for a Greenwood Village lot
sections.html:
Water quality and yield deserve separate checks. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 364 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 126 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 5 historic mine features. These mapped sites do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to review the well’s location, test existing water, and ask the county or Colorado DWR about applicable records.

Septic placement, drainage, access for a rig, and the building envelope also matter. A well that produces water may still be a poor fit if the lot cannot separate the well from septic components or provide reliable drilling access. Confirm household-use rights, permit conditions, and any augmentation requirement before designing the house. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for new use.

sections.heading: Before you buy or build near Greenwood Village
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not a citywide average. Search nearby DWR permits in Greenwood Village, Cherry Hills Village, Cherry Creek, Centennial, Holly Hills, Inverness, and Acres Green. Compare depth, aquifer, casing, static level, and yield records. The local median is encouraging, but the 17% share of wells at 600 feet or deeper shows why a contingency for a deeper hole belongs in the budget.

For an existing home, inspect the well equipment, request recent water testing, and verify the permitted use. For raw land, have a Colorado well contractor review access, siting, septic separation, electrical routing, and likely drilling depth before closing. Fractured-bedrock results can be unpredictable, and a dry or low-yield hole is a real project risk. Treat a neighbor’s successful well as useful evidence, not a promise.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Greenwood Village?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Greenwood Village is 35 feet, and the middle half runs from 23 to 120 feet. Still, 17% of recorded wells are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 2,485 feet, so a parcel-specific estimate should use nearby permits and construction reports.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Greenwood Village?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,800 to $2,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $7,800 to $14,400. Deeper drilling or difficult access can raise the final price.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Greenwood Village?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 15.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 10.0 to 124.8 gallons per minute. Fifty-seven percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, but 3% report less than 1 gallon per minute. Only 230 wells report yield, so request the individual well’s test results.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Greenwood Village?
faq.a: The mapped area includes 364 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 126 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not establish contamination at a specific home. Test the actual well, review nearby environmental records, and retest when conditions or land use warrant it. A well permit alone is not a water-quality guarantee.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Greenwood Village?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a decline: static water level was 18 feet below surface in the 2010s and 17 feet in the 2020s. Only 81 wells report static water level, so this is limited evidence. Check the specific well’s static level, pumping history, and seasonal behavior before drawing a conclusion about a property.
